How much do you trust Wikipedia?

I have history books I trust.

Wikipedia I take at 75%, and I can look elsewhere for confirmation.

It's the most comprehensive source of information accessible to us, period. Even if it is not completely trustworthy, I've learned a lot from it, even more than I learned from years of formal academic schooling.

Obviously, there is bias, but there is going to bias in any source of information. Still, you can often read between the lines to get to the truth.

Furthermore, for current event stuff, you can see where exactly they have sourced the information by checking the footnotes. So if you believe the sources are questionable, then you can just disregard the info.

Miles Mathis does a great job of showing how to read between the lines on Wikipedia, and coming to some pretty remarkable insight. Some of his conclusions can be far fetched (especially lately), but still worth looking into.

It depends on the topic. I trust it for descriptions of mathematical topics, most zoological topics, most astronomical topics, basically most hard sciences which are not heavily politicized.

I do not trust it with history other than as a starting point if I want to know what mainstream, leftist historians are currently pushing. I do not trust it with any topic where there are cultish fanbases (so many gaming, anime, and similar topics are very suspect). I do not trust it with anything touching on politics or social issues (and this includes even articles which should be based on hard science).

I barely trust them. When someone writes a book, they are doing it for profit usually. Encyclopedia Britannica is a product designed to be very expensive under the guise of assuming you're paying for quality.

You get very little for contributing to a Wikipedia article just for the sake of doing it. You're not going to get any money from Wikipedia. If you're knowledgeable in a subject enough to write a proper book or academic resource, why would you do it pseudo-anonymously on Wikipedia? So it ends up gathering a lot of people who aren't qualified to write academic papers or books and are instead doing it for other reasons.

The flaw of the wiki model is completely obvious with Wikitravel. It started out with hobbyists writing ok articles. I haven't used it in years, but the last time I used it, there were clearly non-native English speakers trying to hype up their own locations.

Wiki's primary encouragement for contributing is personal gain. You want to edit articles to push your politics, promote yourself or a product, harm a competitor, etc. Traditional encyclopedias aren't perfect, they have issues. But at the end of the day, the people who make them are doing so to establish themselves as the most authoritative source so they can charge more money for them. Rarely you will find a resource on Wikipedia that's just done by autistic fans who are really devoted to something. But those are extremely rare.

Highly variable by article. Here's a rough classification from best to worst.

A: Non-controversial topics in natural sciences: These are often written by subject area experts who know their topic well, but don't have an emotional or financial stake in how it's presented. Since nobody else cares or understands enough to get in the way, and since the experts aren't arguing with each other, you get a good, stable article.

B: Popular culture fads: These tend to get written by their fans. As with group A, they know the subject and get left alone by everyone else who doesn't care. Although they're generally well-intentioned, they don't write as well and don't try to be unbiased. Their articles often contain a lot of irrelevant detail. Transportation articles like minor subway stations also fall into this category.

C: Things that somebody is trying to make money off of: Public relations and marketing firms look at Wikipedia the way a logger looks at a National Forest -- as a very valuable natural resource to be harvested and sold to their clients before someone else cuts it down to sell to their clients. These people will eventually destroy Wikipedia. Most articles about existing corporations, non-profits, and the people involved with them are junk. The ones with active edit histories are still reliable for basic facts, but there are thousands of Wikipedia pages about defunct orgs still written in present tense simply because no one from the company came back to update the article about its demise, and nobody else knew they ever existed.

D: Religion, politics, and similar articles that attract partisans and nutcases: These usually end up locked down and biased in favor of whichever group of partisans and nutcases has more successfully infiltrated the ranks of Wikipedia Admins and Arbitrators. Reading the page history and the talk pages to see what got removed is often more enlightening than what the article itself.

F: Schools: These often start out at about level C, but less professionally written, but are so frequently vandalized by their own bored students updated the names of the administration and adding themselves to the notable alumni sections, that they can't be trusted for anything. Town and villages, especially in Africa and Asia also belong in this category.

As for a target, I've got THE target you can make for very little. Go buy a 6'-8' treated post. 4x4 or 5x5, whichever. Then cut about 5"-6" slices until you have enough to make something like a 4ft by 4ft square target. Lay them all down on a plywood or OSB board of the same size.
